About

An opinionated, independent, remote-only job board.

Four people in Berlin and Lisbon, profitable since 2021, no investors, no plans to "scale up the platform side." Just a job board run by people who actually do remote work.

Our story

How it started

Remote Roost started in late 2018 because Mira and Henrik were both, in different ways, burned by the same thing. Mira had left a strong design role in Stockholm for what was advertised as a fully-remote senior position at a US fintech — only to find out, three weeks in, that "remote" meant "fly to San Francisco for two weeks a quarter and the all-hands isn't on Zoom for the people who aren't there." Henrik had taken a Berlin-based "remote-friendly" engineering role and discovered the friendly part stopped at the office door: the decisions all happened in the corridor outside the standup.

They were complaining to each other over coffee in Lisbon — both having ended up there, separately, between jobs — and realized two things at once. First, every existing remote job board was indiscriminate. They took any posting that had the word "remote" in it, including the bait. Second, the kinds of companies that do get remote work right were getting drowned out by everyone else.

So they did the small, obvious thing. They started a tiny job board with one rule: every listing got read by a human before it went live, and listings that didn't meet a minimum bar (real salary band, real location requirement, no hybrid sneak-in) got rejected. The first month had 11 listings. The first year had 380. We're now at 147 active listings on any given day, around 4,500 a year, and we still read every one before it goes live.

Editorial standards

What gets listed, and what doesn't

The version of this on the post-a-job page is for employers. This is the same rules, framed for you, the job-seeker. If we ever post something that breaks these, write to us and we'll pull it.

Every listing has

  • A real salary range (band, not the word "competitive").
  • A specific location requirement (region, country, or timezone window).
  • A statement of the hiring process (at minimum: number of stages).
  • A reachable human at the company's domain.
  • Confirmation that the role is fully remote — not hybrid, not "mostly remote."

We reject (about 14% of submissions)

  • "Remote-friendly" or "remote in [specific city]" postings.
  • Postings hiding the salary band behind a recruiter call.
  • Unpaid take-home work over 3 hours.
  • Vague or fictional locations.
  • Listings from staffing agencies posting for unnamed clients.
  • Companies with a documented pattern of bait-and-switch.

Our take

Remote work, eight years in

The thing we got wrong in 2018 was assuming the world was on a one-way trip to remote-first. The thing the world got wrong in 2022 was concluding it wasn't. The actual shape is messier and, we think, more interesting: most companies are now hybrid in a way that punishes the people who are remote, a meaningful minority are fully distributed and getting good at it, and the gap between those two groups is widening every year.

Our bet is that the second group keeps winning the talent fight — slowly, unevenly, and not in the categories the breathless thinkpieces usually cover. It shows up in lower attrition at fully-distributed companies than at "RTO three days a week" ones. It shows up in the salary spread for senior engineers: the top 25% of remote-only roles now pay more than the median in-office role in the same city. It shows up in who runs the design system at companies you've heard of — increasingly, it's somebody who hasn't met any of their coworkers in person in a year.

What we hear from candidates is that the second-order effects are what surprised them. Remote work didn't give them an extra commute hour — it gave them the ability to take their kid to school, do their job, pick the kid up, and not feel like a worse parent or a worse employee. It didn't make them "more productive" in some legible way. It made them less constantly tired. That's a real thing, and the companies we list are, we think, the ones who treat it as a real thing.

The companies that have figured this out are not the loud ones. They are not "thought leaders." They are mostly companies between 20 and 200 people, often profitable, often boring on the outside, that decided early to write things down, to run meetings as if half the room weren't in the room, and to make decisions in places where decisions are findable later. The boring stuff. The stuff that scales without theatrics.

What we'd like to see less of, from candidates and from companies both: pretending async is a synonym for "no meetings ever" or "you can work whenever." It is neither. Async is "decisions are written down, handoffs are explicit, and your presence in real time is not the unit of trust." That requires a lot of work. Most companies that claim to be async are not, in fact, async. Most companies that are async don't make a big deal about it.

What we'd like to see more of, from the press: stop interviewing the same six CEOs about whether remote work is "over." Talk to the people doing it. Talk to the people hiring for it. Talk to the people who left in-office jobs and would not go back. It's not a debate, it's a labor-market shift, and the people on the ground stopped arguing about it a long time ago. They're just getting on with it.

Timeline

How we got here

Eight years compressed into the highlights worth noting.

2018 · Founded
Mira and Henrik launch a one-page WordPress site from a Lisbon coffee shop. 11 listings in month one. No revenue model yet — listings are free.
2019 · First paid listing
A Belgian SaaS company asks if they can pay to be featured. We invent the pricing on the spot ($150) and a business model accidentally appears. 380 listings this year.
2020 · The COVID year
Volume goes up 4×. We also reject a record number of listings — companies that had been hybrid suddenly claim to be "remote-first." We write the first version of the editorial rubric this year.
2021 · Profitable
First fully-profitable year. Mira moves to working on this full-time. We move off WordPress to a Rails app Henrik writes evenings and weekends. (We still apologize for the WordPress era when asked.)
2022 · Vera joins
First hire. The review queue had been backing up to 3 days and the quality bar was slipping. Vera halves the queue time within a month.
2023 · The RTO year
Big-company return-to-office mandates push a wave of candidates toward remote-only boards. Volume doubles again. We deliberately do not raise prices.
2024 · Sam joins; Pro Pack launches
Hire #2 (the long-debated fifth person). Launch the Pro Pack tier for companies hiring 3+ roles in a quarter. Quietly add invoice billing for European customers.
2025 · 28,000th listing
We hit 28,000 lifetime listings posted. Newsletter crosses 4,500 subscribers. We turn down a third acquisition inquiry without taking the meeting.
2026 · You are here
147 listings active today. Still four people. Still in Berlin and Lisbon (and now Lagos and Bristol). Still rejecting about 14% of submissions.
For the record

Things we don't do, and won't

The clearest way to describe a small business is by what it has decided not to be. Here is what Remote Roost will not become, even when asked nicely.

We don't take a cut of salaries. We don't take referral fees. We don't have an in-house recruiting arm and we never will — the moment we have a stake in who gets hired, our incentives stop aligning with candidates'. We don't run banner ads or sponsored listings dressed up as content. The "Featured" badge is the only paid placement on the site and it is clearly labeled.

We don't use AI to screen applicants and we don't sell our reader data. The newsletter list has never been shared. Job-seeker accounts are anonymous unless you opt in. We don't store applications — when you click apply, you go to the company's own URL or email. We are not a middleman in the hiring process and we don't want to be.

We don't take meetings about getting acquired. We've had three serious inquiries — two from larger job boards, one from a recruiting platform. Each one made it clear that being independent is the whole point. The site exists because we, personally, wanted it to exist. Selling it would defeat the thing.
